entries.title: Article: Eliminating Long-Lived Credentials in GCP with Workload Identity Federation
entries.summary: Long-lived GCP service account keys are secrets that must be managed forever, are hard to rotate, and are easy to leak. Scaling Workload Identity Federation to 120+ production projects shows why it changes how machine identity is approached entirely: keys are secrets to manage, federated identities are trust relationships configured once, gated by attribute conditions. By Shijin Nair
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • Workload Identity Federation (WIF) is not just a security improvement, it changes how you think about machine identity: Keys are secrets you manage, while federated identities are trust relationships you configure.
  • WIF allows external workloads to authenticate to Google Cloud Platform (GCP) without long-lived service account keys, reducing credential exposure and operational overhead.
  • WIF follows the same three-part model across all implementations: a pool, a provider/connector, and a service account binding.
  • Attribute conditions are the critical security gate. Without them, any identity from a trusted provider can authenticate, which is too broad for production.
  • Mandating WIF at project creation rather than retrofitting existing keys scaled cleanly, with legacy no-expiry keys treated as a fixed, shrinking problem rather than something requiring a risky migration.

The Problem I Kept Running Into

Every time I onboarded a new continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) tool or gave a third party access to a GCP project, I ended up doing the same thing: navigating to Identify and Access Management (IAM), creating a service account, downloading a JSON key, and pasting it somewhere as a secret. It worked. But it always felt wrong.

You can configure service account keys with an expiry date; for better security you should. But that creates its own problem. Every time a key expires, you have to generate a new one for the same service account, then track down every system and team using the old key and share the new one with them. In practice, that operational overhead is significant enough that many teams skip expiry entirely and leave keys open-ended, which is a much worse solution. Regardless of expiry, the keys sit in secret stores, environment variables, and sometimes, if someone makes a mistake, in version control. Auditing which key was used when is possible, but it depends on audit logging being enabled in advance. If a key leaks, you often don't know its blast radius until you've dug through those logs.

When I first came across Workload Identity Federation (WIF), my reaction was skepticism. Another IAM abstraction layer? But after implementing it across several production workloads and connecting Harness pipelines, GitHub Actions workflows, and Amazon Web Services (AWS) Lambda functions to GCP, I am convinced it is the right model for machine-to-machine authentication.

This article is not another "what is WIF" overview. Instead, it covers what mandating this approach at scale actually looked like, including how my organization went from zero to 120 projects or more on WIF in six months, a scoping mistake worth watching for in multi-org Harness setups, why we chose impersonation over the direct access that Google recommends as the default, and what actually happens when AWS Security Token Service (STS) proves an identity to GCP under the hood.

What Workload Identity Federation Actually Is

My initial skepticism came from the shape of WIF. Three separate objects must exist before anything works. None does anything useful alone. Compared to downloading a JSON key, that design felt like a lot of ceremony for the same outcome.

What changed my view was realizing that the ceremony is the point. A service account key is a secret you now own and must protect forever. WIF replaces that design with a trust relationship you declare once and never handle again.

The mechanism is straightforward. Instead of handing a credential to an external system, you tell GCP in advance which external identity providers you trust and under what conditions. When an external workload needs access, it presents its own native token to GCP's Security Token Service. GCP validates that token against your configuration and, if it passes, issues a short-lived GCP access token. The job runs, the token expires, nothing is stored and nothing needs to be rotated. The setup has three components.

The Workload Identity Pool

This is a named container in your GCP project that groups external identity configurations. Think of it as a folder that holds your trust configurations. On its own, it does nothing.

The Provider

This connector lives inside the pool and defines the actual trust. You configure one provider per external identity system. The provider tells GCP where tokens come from, how to validate them, how to map their claims to GCP-understandable attributes, and which specific identities are allowed through.

The Service Account Binding

This is the final piece. Once an external identity passes validation, it needs actual GCP permissions. You bind specific pool identities to a service account, and the workload temporarily inherits that service account's IAM permissions.

Workload Identity Federation is not a GCP-only concept. For example, Microsoft Entra Workload ID implements the same idea for Azure, using OpenID Connect (OIDC)-based federated credentials to eliminate stored secrets for external workloads. The underlying trust-relationship model, with the external token in and the short-lived platform token out, carries over. The mechanics in this article, the pool, the provider, the attribute conditions and their Common Expression Language (CEL) syntax, are specific to GCP's implementation.

You can use Workload Identity Federation with workloads that authenticate using X.509 client certificates, that run on AWS or Azure, on-premises Active Directory, deployment services, such as GitHub and GitLab, and with any identity provider (IdP) that supports OpenID Connect or Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) V2.0.

How We Adopted WIF

We did not migrate. That is worth being direct about, because "we retired every key in the estate" is a different and much harder article than this one.

Our environment had hundreds of service account keys with no expiry set, some of which were years old. Retrofitting those keys required coordinating across every team and system holding a copy, with an outage risk at each step and no clean way to prove a given key was actually dead rather than merely unused that week.

So we drew a line at the point of creation instead. As part of a broader cloud modernization initiative, WIF became mandatory for every new GCP project. No new project received a service account key. Deployments ran through Harness pipelines using federated identity, This requirement was enforced at project provisioning rather than left to each team to opt into. Within six months, more than 120 projects were authenticating this way.

The legacy keys did not disappear, but they stopped multiplying. That reframed the problem from an ever-growing surface into a fixed and shrinking one, which made it tractable.

Mandating this change early also had a benefit I did not anticipate. Because every project inherited the same pattern, the scoping conventions were settled once, at the start, rather than diverging across teams. After the first few providers, each new integration was a copy of a configuration we already trusted rather than a fresh design decision.

The OIDC Connector: Teaching GCP to Read External Tokens

Most modern CI/CD platforms support OIDC. When a workflow or pipeline runs, the platform automatically generates a short-lived JSON Web Token (JWT) for that run. This token is cryptographically signed by the platform's own OIDC issuer; it contains claims describing the identity, for example, which repository, which organization, or which pipeline account originated the run.

The OIDC connector is how you teach GCP to understand these tokens. When you configure a provider of type OIDC inside your pool, you define three things.

The Issuer URL

This is the OIDC endpoint of the external platform. GCP fetches the platform's public keys from this URL and uses them to verify that incoming tokens are genuine and unmodified.

Attribute Mappings

This is a translation layer. GCP does not natively understand Harness claim names or GitHub claim names. The mappings tell GCP: "when you see 

assertion.account_id
in the token, call it 
attribute.account_id"
. The reserved mapping 
google.subject = assertion.sub
is always required and becomes the principal identity.

Attribute Conditions

This is the security gate, a CEL expression that filters which identities are actually allowed through. Without this expression, any valid token from the issuer passes. With it, you can restrict to a specific organization, account, repository, or any claim the token contains.

To make this concrete, in a Harness implementation I worked on recently, the attribute condition was:

attribute.account_id == "abcdrfghijklmnop" &&
attribute.organization_id == "my_org_platform"

This configuration dictates that even if someone had a valid Harness JWT from a different Harness account, GCP would reject it at this step. The condition is your last line of defense at the identity layer.

Google's documentation on configuring Workload Identity Federation with other identity providers covers the full range of supported attribute mappings and conditions.

GitHub Actions to GCP

GitHub Actions is one of the most common WIF use cases. Every GitHub Actions job automatically receives an OIDC token containing the repository, branch, workflow name, and environment. No configuration is needed on the GitHub side; it is built in.

The first step is to create the pool and OIDC connector on the GCP side.

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create github-pool \
  --location="global" \
  --project=YOUR_PROJECT

 
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc github-connector \
  --location="global" \
  --workload-identity-pool=github-pool \
  --issuer-uri="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.repository=assertion.repository" \
  --attribute-condition="assertion.repository=='your-org/your-repo'" \
  --project=YOUR_PROJECT

Next, bind the pool to a service account.

gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding deploy-sa@YOUR_PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github-pool/attribute.repository/your-org/your-repo" \
  --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser"

Finally, in the GitHub Actions workflow, add the OIDC token permission and use the google-github-actions/auth action.

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read 
- uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
  with:
    workload_identity_provider: projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github-pool/providers/github-connector
    service_account: deploy-sa@YOUR_PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com

That is the entire setup. No secret is stored in GitHub. The token lasts for the duration of the workflow run and expires automatically.

For the full walkthrough, including Terraform examples and other CI/CD platforms beyond GitHub, see Google's guide to Workload Identity Federation with deployment pipelines.

Harness Pipelines to GCP

Harness also supports OIDC natively. When a Harness pipeline runs, it generates a JWT containing claims for the account ID, organization ID, project ID, and pipeline identifier. The setup follows the same three-part WIF model, with Harness-specific claim names.

The issuer URL for Harness is tied to your account:

https://app.harness.io/ng/api/oidc/account/YOUR_HARNESS_ACCOUNT_ID

The attribute mappings extract Harness-specific fields from the JWT:

google.subject=assertion.sub
attribute.account_id=assertion.account_id
attribute.organization_id=assertion.organization_id
attribute.project_id=assertion.project_id

The attribute condition then locks it to your specific Harness account and org. A common mistake I see is omitting the 

organization_id
check and only filtering on account_id. This is acceptable if your Harness account has a single org, but in multi-org accounts it is too permissive.

When binding the pool to a service account, a 

principalSet
with 
attribute.account_id
rather than a specific subject allows any pipeline within that account to impersonate the service account. If you want tighter control, for example, only a specific pipeline, then use the subject attribute instead, which will be scoped to that exact pipeline run identity.

AWS Workloads to GCP

The AWS implementation is the one that surprises people most. AWS does not use OIDC for its workload tokens, it uses its own format based on AWS STS 

AssumeRole
. WIF handles this format with a dedicated provider type rather than OIDC.

The trust anchor here is an AWS account ID rather than an issuer URL. You tell GCP to trust tokens from this specific AWS account. GCP then validates that incoming tokens are genuine AWS tokens from that account using AWS's own verification mechanism.

How AWS Tokens Work

When code runs on an AWS workload, an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, or an ECS task, AWS automatically gives it temporary credentials tied to an IAM role. These credentials consist of three things:

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
AWS_SESSION_TOKEN

When that workload wants to prove its identity to an outside system, it uses these credentials to call AWS STS GetCallerIdentity. This is an AWS API call that returns a signed response saying: "this request genuinely came from IAM role X in AWS account 123456789".

The key thing is the signature on that response can only be produced by AWS itself. Nobody outside AWS can fake it.

What GCP Actually Does to Validate

When the AWS workload sends its token to GCP's STS, GCP doesn't just take the AWS account ID at face value. Here is what happens under the hood:

Step 1: GCP Receives the AWS Credential Package

The workload sends its AWS access key, secret key, and session token to GCP, not as raw credentials, but packaged as a signed request to AWS STS GetCallerIdentity.

Step 2: GCP Calls AWS STS on Your Behalf

GCP actually makes the GetCallerIdentity API call to AWS itself, using the signed request the workload provided. GCP is essentially asking AWS: "Is this token real?"

Step 3: AWS Responds with the Identity

AWS validates the signature internally and responds with the IAM role ARN and the AWS account ID the token belongs to.

Step 4: GCP Checks the Response Against Your Configuration

GCP looks at the AWS account ID returned and checks. If it matches the account ID you configured in the AWS provider, then the token is genuine. Otherwise, it is rejected.

Implementation

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create aws-pool \
  --location="global" \
  --project=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT

 
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-aws aws-connector \
  --location="global" \
  --workload-identity-pool=aws-pool \
  --account-id="AWS_ACCOUNT_ID" \
  --project=YOUR_GCP_PROJECT

The service account binding for AWS scopes down to a specific IAM role, not just the account:

gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  aws-accessor@YOUR_GCP_PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/aws-pool/attribute.aws_role/arn:aws:sts::AWS_ACCOUNT_ID:assumed-role/ROLE_NAME" \
  --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser"

The AWS workload uses the GCP credential configuration file that is generated via 

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create-cred-config
and sets it as the 
GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
environment variable. GCP client libraries detect this file format automatically and handle the AWS STS token exchange transparently. The workload does not need to know anything about WIF internally.

Google's documentation on Workload Identity Federation with AWS or Azure VMs covers this setup in more depth.

Security Considerations

WIF solves the key leakage problem but introduces its own attack surface if not configured carefully.

Attribute Conditions Are Not Optional in Production

The default behavior (or condition) allows any authenticated identity from the provider to exchange tokens. For GitHub, that allows any public repository on the platform to potentially authenticate to your pool if the issuer URL matches. Always define a condition.

Use principalSet Scoping Carefully

The difference between 

principal://
(a single specific subject) and 
principalSet://
(all identities matching an attribute) has significant blast radius implications. Start narrow, a specific repository or pipeline, and widen only if operationally necessary.

Short-Lived Does Not Equal Zero Risk

WIF tokens typically last one hour. If a token is intercepted within that window, it can be used. Mitigate this by scoping service accounts to the minimum permissions needed and enabling Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Service Controls where applicable.

Audit Token Exchanges

The WIF pool detail page in the GCP console shows a usage graph of successful token exchanges. Enable Cloud Audit Logs on the IAM API to capture token exchange events with full metadata: which subject, which provider, which service account was impersonated. This is the equivalent of your door access logs.

Pool and Provider Deletion Is Not Immediate

Deleting a pool puts it into a thirty-day soft-delete state, restorable with undelete, but token exchanges fail immediately regardless. After thirty days, deletion is permanent. Treat pool management with the same care as deleting a service account.

Comparing the Three Implementations

AspectGitHub ActionsHarnessAWS
Provider typeOIDCOIDCAWS (native)
Trust anchorIssuer URLIssuer URL (per account)AWS account ID
Token issued byGitHub automaticallyHarness automaticallyAWS STS AssumeRole
Key security filterrepository claimaccount_id + org_idIAM role ARN
Workload configgithub-actions/authHarness OIDC settingcred-config JSON file

Direct Access vs. Impersonation Is a Real Choice, Not a Style Preference

Instead of routing through a service account, WIF also lets you grant IAM roles straight to the federated principal on the resource, called direct resource access. Google recommends this as the default: It removes the service account from the flow and keeps each external identity's access visible on exactly the resources it was granted.

This article instead uses impersonation throughout for two concrete reasons. First, an external identity federates once, but often ends up needing access across many projects and pipelines over time. Google's own best practices warn that mapping one identity to multiple IAM principals, which is what happens when the same identity picks up a separate direct-access binding per project, makes it harder to see what it can actually reach. It also creates real risk on offboarding. If a binding is missed during revocation, then access silently persists. Routing everything through service accounts required revoking access was one action instead of an audit across every project the identity had touched.

Second, direct access clears the per-API limitations table for every service a pipeline calls, rather than once at setup. It is also more brittle across VPC Service Controls perimeters. Both are cases where Google points to impersonation as the better fit.

There is one operation where direct access does not just have a limitation, but cannot work at all: Cloud Storage signed URLs. A signed URL is not an authenticated API call; it is a URL you hand to someone with no GCP identity. What makes it trustworthy is a cryptographic signature tied to a specific service account. Producing that signature needs either the service account's private key or the iam.serviceAccounts.signBlob permission, neither of which exists for a bare federated principal. Under impersonation, signing works because your federated token calls signBlob on the service account you are impersonating. Google signs the payload with a key it holds in escrow. This is a narrow case in practice. Most of what these pipelines do is unaffected by it, but it is a hard constraint rather than a preference where it applies.

When WIF Does Not Apply

WIF is the right solution for workload-to-GCP authentication, but it does not cover every scenario. Human users authenticating to GCP should use Cloud Identity or Workforce Identity Federation, a related but separate feature designed for people rather than machines. WIF is specifically for non-human callers: pipelines, services, and automated systems.

Some GCP services and client libraries have limitations with federated credentials. Check the supported services list in the GCP documentation before assuming WIF will work end-to-end. Access Context Manager is one example. Its v1alpha APIs are not yet available to federated identities, even though the rest of the product works normally.

The identity federation products and limitations page lists every product's current level of support. It is worth checking before building against something less common than GitHub Actions or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE).

If you are running workloads inside GCP, on Compute Engine, GKE, or Cloud Run, you do not need WIF. Those workloads already have a first-class GCP identity via the metadata server. WIF is specifically for workloads that live outside GCP.

Conclusion

The shift from service account keys to WIF is not just a security improvement. It changes how you think about machine identity. Keys are secrets you manage. Federated identities are trust relationships you configure. One requires operational discipline to stay secure. The other is secure by design.

The practical consequence is repeatability. Create a pool, add a provider with a tight attribute condition, and bind a least-privilege service account. That sequence held across every integration we did, which is the only reason mandating it across new projects was realistic. A pattern that needs rethinking each time does not scale to a hundred teams.

The zero-credentials-stored outcome is worth the initial learning curve. There is nothing to rotate, nothing to accidentally commit, and nothing that gives an attacker permanent access if intercepted. For any team running CI/CD pipelines or connecting third-party services to GCP, WIF should be the default choice.

entries.title: Podcast: Scott Jenson on Evolving Desktop OS, Local-First, & Agentic UX
entries.summary: In this episode, Scott Jenson, a veteran UX designer known for his work on the Macintosh, Google Maps, and Chrome examines the long-term stagnation of desktop operating systems and the limitations of current mobile and cloud-centric models. By Scott Jenson
entries.content:
In this episode, Scott Jenson, a veteran UX designer known for his work on the Macintosh, Google Maps, and Chrome examines the long-term stagnation of desktop operating systems and the limitations of current mobile and cloud-centric models. The conversation shifts toward specialised "Local-First" software, exploring how we can move beyond the "status quo" of interface design to create more intuitive, powerful, and privacy-conscious computing environments in the advent of the "LLM everywhere" era.

Key Takeaways

  • Desktop operating systems have seen little fundamental innovation in two decades, focusing primarily on ecosystem lock-in rather than enhancing user productivity.
  • While mobile dominates consumer attention, it lacks the depth required for complex productivity. Tablets are specialized for consumption, not creation, and cannot replace the desktop.
  • Local-First architecture addresses the fragility and privacy risks of the cloud-centric era by ensuring data sovereignty and resilience against connectivity outages.
  • Current interfaces rely on stateless direct manipulation. Future operating systems should implement ‘working memory’, context-aware scaffolding that tracks user activity and history.
  • The future of LLM integration lies in embedding intelligence directly into application workflows, moving away from universal ‘chatbots’ toward functional, agentic interfaces.

Subscribe on:

Transcript

Olimpiu Pop: Hello, everybody. I'm Olimpiu Pop, an InfoQ editor. And today I have in front of me Scott Jenson. For those of you, if the name doesn't mean anything, he's probably one of the UX designers that has a lot of impact on your life or the things that you're doing if you're using a MacBook or if you're using an Android phone because you worked on a lot of this stuff. Thank you, Scott, for talking to us.

Mobile vs. Desktop: Productivity vs. Consumption [00:45]

Scott Jenson: Great. I'm happy to be here. Yes, I basically started off at Apple. I worked on the Macintosh System 7. I then worked over and moved over to the Newton, which was a big handheld at the time, got a lot of hype, then moved over to do a lot of desktop work. I ended up working at Google and worked on the first version of Google Mobile Maps. Went over and worked on the Chrome team, had a project called the Physical Web, and then did quite a bit of consulting. I was at Frog Design for a number of years as creative director and worked on some big projects for say HP and Disney. And went back to Google at the end of my career. About two years ago, I left Google. I'm now working on my own.

Olimpiu Pop: I liked one of your talks and the way how you framed the current work that you're doing. You mentioned that you are repenting for your sins in the last period, and that's why a lot of your work is currently in open source. Thank you for taking the energy and time during this period and doing that much exploration. And that's why we are together because you did have, I think almost a year ago, it was a Ubuntu, I think, conference where you spoke about the past, present, and future maybe, but more on the present and future of what UX for desktop means. That got a lot of traction. I think it was last time when I checked, it was half a million views. And then I saw the presentation that you had at Local-First, not that much traction because it's more current than the other one. But what you had different there, you had a couple of ideas that you shared.

Actually, you put your fingers or your ideas, creative ideas into practice, and you provided a couple of ideas how UX can look for desktop and to better organize your work. But let's not get ahead of ourself and take a step back. Let's look a little bit, as you mentioned, you grew to the phases of what desktop means. Let's look at how the UX in the desktop space evolved and maybe touch a bit if you think it's useful on the differences between mobile and desktop. Because even though mobile is around with us for some time now, we are still using desktop and there is no sense of something that will come and replace them, that people try to replace them with the tablets, but that's nowhere near into that term.

Scott Jenson: Well, I think you covered a lot of the key hits I've been talking about over the last couple years. The first one is just that the desktop has basically stopped evolving for the last 20 years. Apple has introduced 12-ish features in the last, say, 15 years, but they're all about making the ecosystem better, universal clipboard or the phone being used in the desktop or AirDrop or things like that.

So the vast majority of the improvement with Macintosh has been to tighten its control around its ecosystem. And the desktop itself has not fundamentally changed. And that transitions to what you were just mentioning about mobile, that a lot of people feel like all the hotness, all the excitement is in mobile. But the point I made in my talk is that mobile won consumers. It didn't win productivity. So back around 2015, all these companies tried, multiple companies.

At Google, they tried this. They called it Tablet Tuesdays. And they was like, "Everybody bring a tablet to work and do all of your work on the tablet". And that was a disaster. It's not that tablets are bad, it's just that tablets are hyper-focused on things like content and gaming and social media. And so mobile and tablets are very good at a very narrow set of things. And so a lot of my work has been trying to say, "Let's not throw desktop out. What is it about desktop that is so powerful? And then how can we inject some of that into mobile?" It's not either or. It's about what's good.

And so I've wanted to both improve mobile, but in the talk I gave at Ubuntu was I also wanted to improve desktop. And my general thesis is that we don't seem to be that excited about improving things. We just accept the status quo. And I gave a couple of ideas on that.

Olimpiu Pop: This thing where you're saying, "Yes, we have tablet and it's useful for some stuff. We have mobile and it's useful for some stuff". But desktop is still king in a couple of categories and that's very useful. That sounds a lot like cloud where you have everything across the board and then regardless of what you're using, you'll have those things. But given that our discussion started around Local-First and what that tries, I had a similar conversation with Adam Wiggins, which is involved both with Local-First, but he also was one of the pioneers of the cloud with Heroku and bringing things between developers. And one of the conclusions of our conversation at that point was we have a tendency as technologies to go from one extreme to the other.

We moved from desktop, we moved all the way to the cloud. And now we are realizing that that abstraction is too much and we missed some of the points and now we have to find a sweet spot. And that doesn't have to be something set in stone, but it'll be probably something like gradient. You're moving left and right depending on what's the scenario or different types of approaches. What's your take on it? How do you feel about it? What will be the things that we can take from, I don't know, maybe mobile, maybe desktop, and what will be the points that we need?

Privacy and Practicality in the Cloud Era [06:21]

Scott Jenson: Again, you touched on many points there. I think the big issue with the cloud. Well, there's lots of things to talk about, but the two big ones is privacy. The idea is that with a cloud, all of your data is with one particular provider. And so this is a well-known issue people talked about. I'm not the first one to mention this. And that's why Local-First gets a little bit worried that you're giving all your data to Google or all your data to Microsoft. And so there's that aspect of it.

But the other one is just simply pragmatic, which is to say we live in a world where you don't always have connectivity. And so how do you continue to work on something if it's in the cloud because you're cut off? And whenever there's an AWS outage, the world seems to always rediscover this fragility of it.

And so there's both a practical and a philosophical reason, I think, for talking about it. But like you said, we don't want to throw the baby out with the bath water. It's not like cloud is inherently wrong. I think Local-First is just trying to build it so it's robust. So I can keep all of my data. You can't take it away from me. And if the cloud goes away, I can continue to work on it. And that feels like a very powerful thing that cuts through all of Local-First.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. And I think, well, it's more heavyweight than what we're discussing, but distribution of load is something quite important. And that goes around in pretty much all aspects of technology in life. I'm just thinking now I'm based in Romania, so that means that we have a huge neighboring country called Ukraine that has a problem for the last couple of years. And that means that if the things are not distributed, they have a huge problem with bombardment just taking out electricity. And I think that's something important also for us. Just distributing stuff, as you mentioned across, we have different copies and there are other problems to that, but that's a whole different conversation, as you mentioned.

So now we have more or less two different trends, if you want. We have the Linux-based family of systems, and I'm thinking now about all the open source distributions or the ones that got forked from them more or less like macOS back in its infancy. And then we have Windows. What do you think? Where does the creativity coming from? Because they have a tendency of copying each other. It's just like a game of tag. Where is the creativity coming from at this point?

Scott Jenson: Yes, that's an interesting question because as a UX designer, what I would say was that Apple was always trying to initially just really solve deeper problems. I worked at Apple for eight years and it was just like, what did people need? And what do we want to do? And I think all tech companies have changed recently, so I don't want to single out any one particular one, but Apple and frankly Google have been, what do we need? It's why I felt like I had to leave Google. It was all about the money. And when I was at Google, we really were a bunch of Boy Scouts and we just wanted to do what was right and the money would follow. It's not like we didn't want money. It was just more like if we did the right thing, it would take care of itself. And it's become so clearly about lock-in.

I mean, what Google has done with Android and Chrome and what Apple has done with Safari and locking out browsers, this is not for users. This is not a user empowerment strategy. This is locking you into our ecosystem so we get our 15% of the revenue. And so yes, I think there's a natural frustration with us, for lack of a better word, late stage capitalism that is showing up in these companies. And I refuse this framing like, well, you got to eat somehow, which just gives up any attempt at ethics or longer-term thinking. And I believe that there is a win-win here. You can make money and you can think longer term.

And in fact, as a UX designer, you're frequently making this play to companies, which is to say, "Yes, if we do this UX work, it's going to cost a little bit more money, but you're going to get brand loyalty, you're going to get less errors, you're going to have less callbacks". So this idea about investing in the future to get bigger returns is at the heart of social democracy. It's a longer term vision that means that we can do the right thing and possibly make money.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes, I agree with you. And while listening to you, an idea was just spinning in my head. It's all nice and cozy thinking about having partially the data that you normally need in your pocket on your phone or tablet or whatever. But the tendency of the standards, and I know that that's a topic that you touched upon, is that the images, for instance, they're so huge. And once you put them on iCloud, they have a tendency of providing very small thumbnails on your phone, but you still need the cloud.

So even though I have what I consider something that is very generous, it's 250 gigabytes of memory, of space on my phone, it's always full. And whenever I want to check a photo, it's like, "Okay, your connectivity is not that great. So please rejoin the Wi-Fi". So I think that's one of the challenges into probably a degrading way of looking at it.

I remember back in the day, 10 years ago, we developed an application and we had a degrading level of quality. For instance, if I was on my mobile phone, the photo was up to a given resolution. And then if I was on a more powerful device like a tablet or even a MacBook, I was providing different degrees. And then that allowed us to zoom in or zoom out depending on the resources that we had. And as you mentioned, there is an ecosystem and everybody tries to lock you in. And I do have to admit that the Apple ecosystem is very well integrated. Everybody else is ears, light ears away. But that's my problem, as you mentioned. A very simple scenario. For me, it happens that I need to send emails from my mobile phone. I download something and I cannot find the file anymore.

And then it's a lot easier to just go to my MacBook. But I think these are the points that you had as well. And going back to desktop, what's the real problem or how you call it? The curse of direct manipulation, I think you referred to it. What are the building blocks that you were starting when we're looking at desktop?

The Curse of Direct Manipulation [12:53]

Scott Jenson: Yes. Well, the previous point you made about the downloading a file and then not being able to find it on your phone, that is a fundamental problem of mobile because what mobile did was it hid effectively files within each application. So if I want to edit a file in another application on mobile, it's nearly impossible. The only way I can do it is to share it to the other application, which often makes a copy. And there is a file manager, but most apps don't use it. In fact, I have a whole blog series about this and how we can have the best of both worlds. We can have the simplicity of hiding files within applications, but we can expose them as files. That's a separate conversation about just evolving the mobile system to be more file-friendly, but keeping this whole self-contained model that makes them so much simpler.

But now going back to your curse of direct manipulation, I used that kind of with my Alan Kay quote that, "Perspective is worth 80 IQ points". And so by understanding a little bit more about what the desktop has historically done, it gave us perspective to figure out what we wanted to do to improve it. And so the idea there was that direct manipulation is stateless. You cut, you paste, you type, you open, you close. And there are all these atomic elements that let you manipulate a document. It's all good. No one's complaining, but it's by design stateless. It doesn't remember what you did. It has no history of what you've done.

And so I used that as my perspective to say, "What would happen if we had an operating system that actually remembered a little bit more of what you did?" And then I had three different prototypes that kind of showed what that was like because that would allow effectively a little bit more stuff to happen and gives us support.

Because to me, the whole purpose of an operating system is to support the user doing work. And direct manipulation is one level of support, but then the next one is this ability to help me maintain my context so I can come back from lunch and I can keep working.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. So taking a step back, it's something that just circled in different environments. So people are saying, "Okay, data is the new oil", and stuff like that. So that's kind of true also for us because in the end, if you get a laptop and doesn't have anything on it's just a machine that is very powerful, but doesn't have the ability. Once you have an operating system on it, you have a collection of applications that allow you to do basic stuff. But once you start using it for you, you have files and all those aggregated. But if you'll open the downloads folder, for instance, that's crazy. It'll be impossible.

And what you mentioned and what you underline now as well is it should be an extension of ourself, our brains, and have also a working memory, some kind of metadata that will allow you more context. And the index is the facility to which we are mentioning to do that. It'll allow you to make things a lot easier and then just resume at different points and then avoid the different types of systems that you need to just do by hand.

Scott Jenson: Yes, exactly.

Olimpiu Pop: You had also a couple of suggestions. You didn't just put the finger on the wound, but you had a couple of proposals, three of them, if I remember correctly. What do you think at this point would make our lives as users of desktop easier? What would be the options that we have on the table?

Scott Jenson: Well, yes, I have a whole talk I can give on that one if you want. But no, the-

Olimpiu Pop: Go ahead.

Three Prototypes for Future Desktops: Spatial, Episodic, and Associative memory model [16:33]

Scott Jenson: No, no, no. But the three prototypes that I showed at the Local-First Conference was about this idea of effectively working memory. The first one was about trying to not be blinkered by the small screens on mobile or frankly, even laptops. And so imagine we had a bigger screen and what could we do with that? And so I had effectively a window manager that allowed you to spread things out so that you had a wide range. And that gets into human perception and how it's very easy for the human eye to look left and right on the horizon and see things in the distance. And so the idea was to have all of the activity that you're doing spread out in a very helpful way that gives you the ability to find things quickly.

I have a lot of issues with people in the Linux community because they are very smart and they're very organized, and that creates a certain type of very rigid software. And the example I gave is virtual desktops. Virtual desktops are very powerful, but they only really work if you're really smart and really organized. And I think a lot of the world is very organic and messy. We all have desktops where things are piled on it. And so I kind of wanted to have a windowing system that was kind of the anti-Linux approach, which was just more organic.

So that was the first one was a window manager that spread everything out. But the other one was to say that we've all been in a situation where you cut and paste something and it's lost because you cut something else on top of it. And yes, all operating systems now have a clipboard history, but we don't really use it. They're kind of a pain. It's like, "Oh, it's the seventh thing down". Or you could, in theory, go into one field and cut every single field out and go to another field and paste them all back in again. But that's nearly impossible. It's tedious. It's just so hard to cut.

So the idea was to say, "How could we elevate this whole copy-paste history model?" So I created a system where a little bit like Obsidian, we had a little side drawer, and you could put all of your clipboard history in there or the files that you're working on or sub-things. It was meant to be effectively a little mini context window that allowed you to store all your data for that particular project. And you could open and close it like a file, but it acted like a folder. And so it was meant to be a way for you to have working memory of that stuff.

And then the final one was more of a history that was totally stolen from a classic paper in the '90s called Lifestreams. And the idea was to say, well, what have I been doing the whole day? Just give me a ribbon of everything I've been doing, but provide some clever visualizations. Because once you give someone some scaffolding, a memory scaffolding, it's like, "All right, that's what I did right before I talked to Olimpiu", or "This is what I did before lunch, this is what I did". And it gives you a little bit of a structure and you can find things effectively by adjacency. And so these aren't the only three things that we could be talking about, but it is an attempt at me to articulate and give examples of how we can have an operating system go well beyond what it's been doing today. And I hope it got people excited.

Olimpiu Pop: Okay. So we are looking about the working memory and how the things are being done and different perspectives on top of that. One of them, as you mentioned, was spatial and that allows you to organize it in a different way, but not in the way with the virtual desktops we have. Because my feeling is that always when I'm looking at virtual desktops, it feels that I have my ski suit on and I have so many pockets, but I'm not ever able to find the car keys or anything else, especially when I'm wearing the ski gloves. That's one. And then that allows you one important aspect that for me it was really impressive was the fact that even the smaller files are useful. So meaning that you can see the data there and you can just use them. Well, for instance, you had an example of a music player and then that's depending on the way how it's zooming in or zooming out, it just changes shape and is still useful.

The other one is in terms of a timeline of what we actually worked and then allows you to look at the things differently or the clipboard being organized in an associative manner where you have different things that are grouped in the way that it's better. What do you think other things that would be useful just as guidelines like best practices? You mentioned you have more, so if there is anything that needs to be brought to light.

Scott Jenson: Well, my overall thesis is the desktop and frankly mobile have gotten frozen in time. And all I want us to do is to try a little harder, to just explore a little bit. So I've written on my blog, I have the future of files and the presence of files that talks about how we can extend mobile. I've done work in the past with Google. I did a project called Eloquent, which is also on my blog that talks about how we could significantly improve text editing on mobile. And then of course, these three concepts I just did on the desktop.

So all I want us to do, my primary goal here is to say there's so much we could be exploring and the world is not set in stone. But so often people think that I want to blow everything up. And there's a crowd of people that says, "It's taken us 30 years to get to this point. Don't blow it up". And I'm like, "Oh, I don't want to blow it up". I mean, things are always changing and we're not going to use the same desktop 50 years from now. Something's going to change. And right now, the way things are looking is we're just going to let Apple hand us the keys to the future because they're going to define what we want to do. And they clearly aren't earning that right. And frankly, neither is Google.

Now I know I'm becoming a little bit more of a radical here, but I mean, my point is to say let's appreciate that there's more to do. And so I gave you three examples. I know there's a gajillion more. And so I don't have anything specific other than those three. But what I am doing is I'm actually trying to turn my prototypes into real code because that also helps.

So the last one I gave you, the live streams that shows me, I've now got it written as a Chrome extension and as a Swift extension. And it's capturing desktop events and it's capturing Chrome events and it's putting it together into a single thing. And I'm going to be giving another talk in September at KDE, and I'm hoping to have it done in time for that. And then I'll open source that, of course, so everybody can play with it. And it raises, by the way, all sorts of privacy issues. But the goal right now is to just try and to see if it's powerful and if it's helpful. And then if it is, then we have to then have further conversations because there is this tension between a system that remembers and does things for you is also a privacy risk. How do you navigate that? And how do you make sure that that's done in a way that's protective of the user? And so that there's a deeper conversation to have there.

Olimpiu Pop: So we are looking forward to your work. Good luck with getting it in time in September. There is not that much time until then, so best of luck with that. And I'll try to add another point based also on the conversations we had and also on your talks. And that's standards. Because now there are a couple of ecosystems, and I'm just thinking now about Apple. I would've stayed away from that. But you did mention earlier AirDrop. And my feeling is that AirDrop is such a great technology, especially when you have people in the proximity and you don't want to go all the way to the cloud and send them on different type of messaging apps. But that works only in the Apple ecosystem.

Scott Jenson: That recently changed. Now Android basically has figured that out and so now it works.

Olimpiu Pop: And that's where I wanted to get to, is the fact that there is a lot of effort on the European Union side to just open that up, to create the standard based on it. AirDrop started it. And it seems that the points regulation is useful as well. Do you think standards is also an important aspect to just have this bridge across different technology gaps? Is it something worth to keep in mind?

The Role of Regulation and Standards [24:40]

Scott Jenson: Oh, absolutely. But whenever you say the word standards, every tech bro in the room will stand up and yell, "You're killing creativity". And so I want to make sure we acknowledge that this is a challenging issue, but say for example, getting Apple to get rid of the lightning connector to go to USBC, that would've never happened if it hadn't been for the EU. And so that was, I think, very good pressure. And again, it shows the fact that from an e-waste point of view, it's the right thing to do to have one universal connector, but it was not in Apple's best interest. It was in the world's best interest. I wouldn't call that a standards conversation. I would just call that kind of a compliance conversation.

And so I do think that there is a bigger role for governments to force companies to think longer term. And I'm going to go back to my radical roots here about late-stage capitalism. It's not that these companies are necessarily evil as much as people like to say they are. I like to say that they are amoral. They're not immoral. They just don't care. They literally only care about the very, very short-term effects, which is why we have global warming and other things as well.

So to me, the way of framing it is what's the longer term goal? Because there's money involved. It costs money to think longer term. And so how do we do that in a way that is fair to these companies, but frankly, is also fair to us? And because I think the vast majority of the decision-making has been only what's fair to the companies, it's been extremely one-sided. So I do believe it's time for a little bit of pushback.

Olimpiu Pop: I would normally refrain from having these kind of comments, especially in the time-bonded context, but you mentioned radical twice already, so I have to mention my radical perspective as well. You're totally right that companies tend to look only at their interest, but that interest is fueled by our comfort because we have a tendency and you can see that all across as humans we'd have, okay, it's a lot easier to bookmark a page. But rather than bookmarking it and being organized, and that gets us to the initial point, we'll use Google search engine. And that's obviously something that goes all across the internet. It's burning fuel and so on and so forth. And now with LLMs, that's even more so.

Scott Jenson: Agreed.

Olimpiu Pop: Ethical aspects, environmental aspects, and so on and so forth. So if we would be more concerned about the future, because the general population will be the most affected by climate change and all the other problems, the companies will have to stand up to their standards. And you can see those points mainly across the last couple of months when there is this sovereignty movement in Europe and where we just realized that we do half things as well. And I'm happy to see that we still have people that are aligned across the pound in terms of what are the European, the Western values and what do we think to just make sure that greed is not the only thing that is fueling technology and everything else.

Scott Jenson: No, I completely agree. And there's multiple forces involved. So we talked just a few minutes ago, we talked about the role of governments to force these things, but also there's the role of technology. For example, what's going on right now with LLMs and the big data centers and so forth. There is likely going to be a technological force that's outside of the governments, which is to say we're going to, over the next five years, have machines that are significantly more powerful, and we're going to have open source local models that can run locally. And this mirrors what's happened throughout the history of technology, whether you're going server side. We went from mainframes to laptop, mini computers. And from mini computers, we went to cloud and we went back to phones.

Beyond Chatbots: Agentic UX [28:28]

And so this idea of going cloud and local and cloud and local has repeated itself throughout history. And I think we'll see the exact same cycle with LLMs. Just yesterday I was trying to do some coding using a local model and it was pretty terrible, but I had to try. But I did switch to an open coding agent and I used DeepSeek and it was shockingly good.

Now, DeepSeek has its own issues. I'm not trying to say it's perfect, but I mean I'm saying we can see the vector. And so as we get a more ethically trained model, which still I don't think that mark has been hit, they all have ethical issues right now. But the point is if we get an open source model that we can run locally, that provides, I think, a fantastically interesting opportunity to switch power away from these big guys too. So there's lots moving. That's interesting.

Olimpiu Pop: Thank you, Scott, for moving the direction towards LLMs because I know your opinion and I align with that because they are at points immoral and they are a terrible disaster for the green footprint, but they're very useful at this point and they'll be able to accelerate it. And now as you open Pandora's box, I have to ask, the guys from Google tried to make everything a webpage with ChromeOS. Well, that didn't take off. Now the guys from OpenAI want to make a small box with just one button and that's it. Is the discussion that we just had useful in the context that everything will be a chat window and everything else will be just typing in?

Scott Jenson: Okay. How much time do you have? The short answer is hell no. And I think as a UX designer, I mean, again, I try to write my thoughts down. So on my blog, I've got a post called Boring. Boring is good. And I think that there is a lot of ways in which we can use LLMs that are smaller and easier, but also we need to understand that intelligence is inherently social. It's a construct that you and I agree on as to what is intelligent. And so much of what we do that is work is actually part of our cultural construct. It's not a mathematical concept of intelligence. It's something that we share as a society. And the same thing applies to LLMs and work. So much of the work is more nuanced, it's got context. And so I do believe that we're going to get more LLM-based support, but it will move towards the problem.

And slapping a chatbot and everything is going to become the first resort of losers. I mean, yes, you can do it and there is some value to it, but I do believe that having the LM built into your problem is more work, but it will allow you to do far more interesting work. So I don't want to go into the details of the specifics, but I do believe that we will get past this chatbot phase as more and more apps are written. But to be clear, it's not as easy. It's cheap to throw a chatbot on.

Olimpiu Pop: Okay. In my evil moment when I was working for a company where dollar was king or where euro was king, I was trying to frame the offer of the company during the takeoff of the L&M. And what I was pushing for was augmented user experience, augmented interfaces. So at points, as you mentioned in our previous conversation where, I don't know, you want to find the right temperature balance with the voice interface, that can be quite problematic when you can be a knob, like just going left and right a bit more, a bit less. It could be frustrating. And that's the feeling also with LLMs at points. But what I think an LLM can do is provide the mechanism at a given point of time where you want to fast onboarding.

Let's say you have an accountant, 20 years of experience, he worked his whole life into a given tool, a given software. He's used only with that. He knows what to do. He moves next day to another one and he doesn't know what to do, but he knows exactly what he should ask. So that, from my perspective, is a good way of looking at it. And it can be voice, it can be a couple of buttons, it can be a chat window. And that's a good way of interacting with an LLM that will provide you the exact tables and charts that you would imagine. And that will be a lot faster than low-code from my perspective.

Scott Jenson: Oh, yes. I mean, just the other day I had a whole bunch of data and I just said, "I want to organize this, but not quite sure". And he goes, "Oh, you should probably use a pivot table". And I'm like, "Well, what's a pivot table?" Because I'm not a big spreadsheet guy, and it explained what it was. And now it still was chat-based. And so what I would challenge these systems to do is to then move to the next step, which is to say, "Okay, I'll actually input the pivot table for you". And in fact, actually, I take it back. I went to Gemini and I asked about it as a pivot table. And so I went into Google Sheets and I take it back. It built a pivot table for me. And so that's what I mean by going into the app and doing more of that.

So yes, I think that there are lots of ways to do that. And I find myself really leaning into the education side of things, which is to say once I learned that, I said, "Okay, now tell me about pivot tables. Why are they there and how do they use?" And it gave me a little mini-documentary. Now, to be fair, this is entirely a chat-based interaction. So I don't want to say chat-based is entirely useless, but I'm trying to draw the distinction between learning and doing. And I think we're going to be doing more doing as these things get more mature.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. Well, it's being refined. I think last year I had a conversation with the guys from Ideal and they had a lot of research into the AI space and they did multiple things, bringing together QR codes, LLMs, dots on pictures and all that stuff. And they tried different mechanisms and different aspects. And I think it's a whole creative evolution, but probably we'll see what comes next as long as we remain creative, as you mentioned. We just try to push ourself into finding the right balance and the right tool.

Scott Jenson: Before we go, I want to make sure that we don't go down this naive path of just adding more tools to the AI because what I just said implied that I just wanted to have more skills and then I could talk to it and it'll just do things for me. Whereas the example I gave in my boring post was about a company that I don't want to encourage them. I'm not trying to recommend them, but it's called Napkin AI where you would talk to it, but it would produce effectively an intermediate artifact. And a lot of the options were built into the user interface.

So in other words, it gave you a whole bunch of choices and each one had alternatives that you could explore. And it was a classic UX. It's like, do you want this one or this one, this one? So you could have talked about it, but my point is a lot of the AI's options revealed itself into classic UX elements.

And so that's quite separate from throwing more skills at a chatbot approach, which is I think the only hammer that these systems can swing is to just throw more skills into the chatbot. So that's the distinction I want to make.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes, most probably just listening to you, what I think I will deem useful, especially in ideation phases as you mentioned, is the ability of switching dynamically between different environments. We started this conversation, but if I'll tell you about, "Scott, I want this kind of frame and with that, that and that", probably it'll be a lot easier to just take a white paper, just draw on it, and then just add colors and so on and so forth. So probably that would be a more morphic ability of doing it, but we'll have to see how things are evolving.

Scott Jenson: Well, yes. And I think it's one of the reasons why UX designers are getting so excited about using coding agents because it means that we can see the results of the coding immediately. And so when I'm working on a more creative idea like this timeline, I've done the research, I have the UX, I know what I want, but there's a lot of details as to how it should be presented to the user in a very nuanced way that just requires a lot of iteration. And what effectively agentic coding allows a UX designer to do is to explore their prototypes significantly faster.

How LLMs Enable Designers to Showcase Their Ideas [36:56]

So yes, I'm using a chatbot to write code, but then I'm playing with the code to say, what am I learning and what's different? And I know multiple designers who are extremely excited by this new switch. It doesn't replace programmers either, by the way. It just allows the UX designer to play at a much, much higher speed than they were before. And I think it actually produces significantly higher quality just because you can try so much and you can fail so much that it gives you that opportunity. So there's a lot of power there.

Olimpiu Pop: What I feel is that before I was limited by the knowledge of using particular tools. For instance, if I was deploying something to the cloud, I used, I don't know, GCP or Azure or whatever because I knew it and that was the ones. But there are other ones out there now. It's just an abstraction point. And even if it's not ideal, and that's the same thing with UI. I don't know, I used React. Now I have the ability of using other frameworks easily that I like how they look or even just go and say, "I like the way how those things are looking. Make me something similar, but tweak it in that way". And that is a lot easier to get to the point that you want.

Now about the quality, that's a whole different perspective and that's where things need to be improved. I'm just thinking about the issues, both on OpenAI or Anthropic where they had agents that just went through the guardrails and just created havoc on the internet. So let's hope for a beautiful future.

Scott Jenson: I guess the closing point I'd like to make is that my mindset is not that these are the answers. It's more that these are the problems and I just want us to see the problems. So often when I talk about the fact that the desktop is dead, I get people to go, "But it's a standard. Why do you want to blow things up, Scott?" And I'm like, "No, can we see that we have so much more that we have to do?" So that's all I want to focus on is to see the problems, get excited by them, and to explore new solutions.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. So it's about the evolution and we should not comply with the status quo because it's something that we got used to. We have to get out on the comfort zone and just move out and make things better.

Scott Jenson: It's surprising how this feels so conservative or the world's gotten so conservative.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes, that's sad. I remember at some point I was reading an article about the movies and music becoming so boring. All of them are just copycats of the other ones because somebody just looking to the numerical part, just took out the soul, took the creative out, and everything became money. We should take a step back, look at the problem, improve it, and then hope for a better future.

Scott Jenson: Exactly.

Olimpiu Pop: Thank you, Scott. Have a great day.

Scott Jenson: Thank you. Enjoyed it. Bye-bye.

entries.title: Presentation: Running AI at the Edge: Running Real Workloads Directly in the Browser
entries.summary: James Hall discusses the strategic and technical imperative of moving AI workloads from cloud providers to local edge devices. He shares practical approaches using WebGPU, Transformers.js, and DuckDB to achieve near-native performance in JavaScript. Through real-world case studies, he explains how to minimize data privacy risks, optimize browser inference, and build rigorous evaluation suites. By
entries.content:
Transcript

James Hall: I'm going to give you a little bit of an intro to myself, some background, just to give you some context of the kinds of things and stuff that I've been working on. I'm going to talk about, why bother? What's the point of running stuff locally? I'm going to intersperse all this with a bunch of demos, so you can actually see and feel how some of this is looking at the moment. I'm going to try and explain at a high level how some of this stuff works, and hopefully give you the pointers that you need to know when you should be using it. I'm also going to give you plenty of pitfalls and takeaways. We've got lots of battle scars. We've made lots of mistakes, so hopefully you can learn from mine.

Background

Just a little bit of background. I started a tech consultancy 15 years ago. We basically build digital products for our customers. We've been given all sorts of weird and wonderful briefs, from street lighting to remote unlocking cars to AI dashboards. There's a big wealth of stuff in there. My background, I've been doing weird and wonderful things with JavaScript for a long while. Just to give you a sense of how much I enjoy bending browsers out of shape. In 2012, I ported a SPC700 emulator. The sound chip inside the SNES, you can actually emulate that. This was very early Emscripten days, so you could actually port C++ to JavaScript. Playing around with lots of Uint8s and massive arrays of numbers. I actually made this work with the then very new and shiny Web Audio API, which, yes, I surprised myself, really. Most people would look at this kind of project and go, what's the point?

It's really good to find the edges of things, like these kinds of experimentation projects. In 2009, so going even further back, I wrote a library called jsPDF, which is haunting me to this day, and has actually had a massive spike in downloads recently. What you can only assume is people vibe coding invoice generation software, or God knows what. Yes, hundreds of emails a day, lots of open PR requests. I was automatically closing PRs way before people got grumpy with AI. This has led to lots of fun, interesting projects and conversations. I'm glad I wrote it, but I hate PDFs. I'm also an external advisor to an AI recycling project.

The other advisor is the head of the UK Fashion Textile Association. We're trying to figure out how we can reduce waste from textiles using automatic sorting. We've been very keen on AI and the application of it for a long while. Right from the street lighting projects, where we were doing automatic detection of faults and predictive maintenance. We really like it when we can actually figure out how the math and the actual application maps to the real world. We've been running events to get people out, get people talking about different applications.

My first exposure to LLMs was actually working for a startup. We made a web browser for them in Kotlin and some React in there. We actually embedded an LLM into the web browser to do automatic tagging and categorization. This was before ChatGPT came out. We had to go to OpenAI and say, this is the app we're building. This is what it does. These are the risk areas that we see. They were very careful about approving each and every use case. Obviously, as soon as ChatGPT was launched, floodgates opened, and they didn't really care anymore, probably because money. It was a very interesting process. We learned a lot doing that. We also launched an LLM-based compliance platform. This won Tech Innovation of the Year. We learned a lot about chatbots. I also know now a lot about why you wouldn't want to build them. Yes, lots of battle scars from this.

We ended up building lots of systems that are now commonplace. We ended up writing our own LLM evaluation and observability platform as part of the product. We also discovered that users interacting with chatbots, because they're so open-ended, you need to draw them into a railroaded experience. We came up with this idea of checklisting. We had our own version of structured outputs, which was very rudimentary to try and put people down a certain path. We learned a lot doing this. We got picked up by a large iGaming company in the UK. We were working with the Timeform team on blending ML models with LLMs. We effectively took over a proof of concept that Amazon Web Services had done. There, they were not able to confidently predict the order of the horses to any degree. I think their F-score was about 0.5, 0.6, a little better than random.

We were able to get that to about 0.9 in a couple of weeks by blending lots of different techniques together. We learned a lot through that project. A lot of where this talk's content is coming from is some of the thinking with some of the new organizations we're working with. A lot of it is industrial IoT. Lots of data. How do we make sense of it? How do we plot it? How do we measure what the trends are? That gives you a bit of background on where all this framing is from and where my brain is sort of at.

Local vs. Cloud

I'd like to talk to you a little bit about the differences between local and cloud. I think a lot of people today will default to cloud because it's the easiest option. It has the strongest models and it is the path of least resistance. A lot of people are picking up these providers, signing their agreements, and sending all of their data to these companies, including their customers' data. The problem with this kind of setup is that end users are increasingly opening up more and more of their personal information without any real thought about the consequences of that. I'm a little bit worried about logging platforms within these organizations. What are the checks and balances for employees looking at data? Can we really trust companies to do what they say they're going to do if they're compelled by the U.S. government to open up logs, for example?

Do you have any control over that? This is where I'm starting to get a little bit worried. This is where these downsides of server-side inference come in. It's not just a privacy concern. There's also low and no internet-connected states. You'd be surprised how, in many countries, the Wi-Fi is very patchy. If you're going on the train, if you're just out of reach of signal. There's also the network latency, which is quite jarring for some applications, especially around real-time video and audio processing. If you're cutting out background noise, for example, you wouldn't want to go from the UK to a data center in Ireland and back and then out to your end user. The cost scales with users, so you become a victim of your own success. Let's say you build something super popular and it relies on the latest and greatest OpenAI model. You get a million users, you've now got a million people to pay for their inference.

I'm going to show you a quick demo of near human-level transcription quality available in JavaScript. The Whisper model was originally produced by the OpenAI team, and they open-sourced the weights.
